6 questions. Click an answer to check it: you will see right away whether it is correct, with a short explanation. Nothing is saved.

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**1.** Why can't we split a time series into a training and a test set at random?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Because the data is too small
- Because the model would learn from the future to predict the past
- Because scikit-learn doesn't allow it
- We can, it works as usual
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
A forecast uses the past to predict the future. With a random split, the training set contains days after the test days: the score would be unrealistically good. Train on the past, test on what comes after.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**2.** What does a moving average of order 7 do?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- It predicts the next 7 values
- It replaces each value by the mean of the last 7 values
- It removes the first 7 values
- It multiplies the series by 7
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
A moving average smooths the series: the random variations cancel out and the trend appears. The larger the window, the smoother, and the more lagged, the curve.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**3.** What is a stationary time series?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- A series that doesn't change at all
- A series whose mean, variance and autocorrelation don't change over time
- A series with a strong trend
- A series without missing values
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
Many classical models assume stationarity. A series with a trend is not stationary; differencing it ($X_t - X_{t-1}$) often makes it stationary.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**4.** What are the components of a Prophet model?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Only a trend
- A trend, seasonalities (daily, weekly, yearly) and holiday effects
- An autoregressive part and a moving average
- A neural network
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
$y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + \varepsilon_t$: trend, seasonality and holidays, plus noise. `plot_components` shows each of them.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**5.** In the Netflix project, the model retrained one month into the Covid crisis is **worse** than the one trained before. Why?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Because it has less data
- Because it has just seen a sudden drop and a rebound, and can't tell which one will last
- Because Prophet can't handle stock prices
- Because of a bug in the code
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
Right after a shock, the recent data is contradictory. The model needs some time, that is, data, to learn the new situation: with two months of crisis data, the error falls to about 4%.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**6.** You want to add the temperature as a regressor to forecast electricity consumption. What do you need?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Nothing more: Prophet finds it
- The temperature for the future dates too, for example from the weather forecast
- Only the past temperatures
- The temperature of the test set, measured afterwards
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
A regressor must be known when the forecast is made. Using values measured afterwards (or the real future price of another stock) is leakage: the score would be too optimistic.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-score}
